maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair there is a matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house which I consider to be serious and important, otherwise I would not discuss it at this time. I refer to the strike that has been in progress in Asbestos, Quebec, for some two months. According to reports in French language newspapers-which by the way are not carried in the English-speaking section of our press-it would appear that it is about time the federal government was made aware of what is taking place.
The strike was merely to establish elementary rights which have been granted by law in practically every province to workers who have organized under the law and have established bargaining agencies. The basis of the strike was, first, a request for increases in wages to meet the increased cost of living, and second, the question of union security.
According to press dispatches which I have had translated from the French, during the first week of the work stoppage everything was orderly and peaceful. Then, without solicitation, as I understand it, by the municipality, the Duplessis government sent the provincial police into the town. Prior to the invasion by the provincial police the workers had been maintaining the fires in the plant, the electrical equipment, and so on, in a proper manner, pending the settlement of the matters in dispute.
According to press dispatches, when the provincial police came in they drove the maintenance men off the plant, thus causing disruption and unnecessary upheaval. The actions of the provincial police in relation to the public in the town leave much to be desired. In case hon. members may think that I am drawing on my imagination I should like to quote English translations of newspaper dispatches.

I have a press dispatch of March 22 by Gerald Pelletier, which appeared in Le Devoir of that day. The translation reads:
Asbestos council protests drunkenness and indecency
Asbestos, February 21-The council of the town of Asbestos protested provincial police conduct in a special assembly of the municipal council held here today.
The protest reads:
Whereas on the 14th of February, 1949, a strike was called in Asbestos in the asbestos industry:
Whereas during the week February 14 to 19 all that occurred was in a peaceful manner in Asbestos:
Whereas during the week of February 14 to 19, on a demand made by the Canadian Johns-Manville Company, a detachment of some 150 provincial policemen were sent to Asbestos, allegedly to protect its properties and salaried employees;
Whereas on their arrival a great number of these policemen were under the influence of alcohol;
Whereas a certain number even rendered themselves guilty of indecent acts in the streets of the town, and also were the cause of disorder in public places;
Whereas in certain cases the provincial policemen used violence against the employees working at caretaking during the strike, and also against the constables of the Canadian Johns-Manville;
Whereas these acts were accomplished without warning and with evident thought of provoking trouble;
It is unanimously resolved by members present to protest to Mr. Hilaire Beauregard, provincial police director, about the conduct of his men; and that a copy of this resolution be sent to the different radio stations and newspapers for publication.
This supports the observation I made that the municipal council did not request the provincial police; that they were in a position to maintain law and order in the community. From my experience of strikes, and I have gone through quite a number, outside interference is permissible only when the municipal government informs either the federal authorities or the provincial government that outside assistance is necessary to maintain law and order. As I understand it, the fact of the matter is that law and order were being maintained until there was outside interference by the provincial police.
In further support of that particular contention, there is another story here confirming the assertion that the provincial police are paid a bonus by the Johns-Manville Company of $50 a week each in addition to the regular wages paid them by the provincial government. This story is from the same newspaper, of the same date, and is by the same reporter. It reads:
About that time other facts, no less disturbing, came to the ears of your reporter. We have learned from a very reliable source that Inspector Nobard L'Abbe, of the provincial police, admitted to a meeting of the municipal council that each of his officers received from Johns-Manville a weekly payment of about $50. One guesses that this revelation did not fail to astonish the witnesses. It was objected to Mr. L'Abbe that the police were paid by the taxpayers and they were not considered to be for sale or for rent; otherwise the unions would hire them for their own contingent. But Mr. L'Abbe
Strike of Asbestos Miners was not troubled by the objection. "These are the expenses of the stay which the company is defraying,'' the inspector explained, "and this is a very common procedure employed in many strikes."
The asbestos strike has taught us many things about the provincial police.
I should like to say here, Mr. Speaker- and I am sure the Minister of Labour will agree with me-that this kind of thing in labour relations is at least thirty years behind the times. I do not think that type of action is possible today in any other province. These workers belong to a legitimate union, the Catholic syndicate. I do not think anyone can say that that organization is communistic, socialistic, or has any of the wild-eyed notions that might be attributed to some other sections of the legitimate union movement. They are a part of the legitimate trade union movement of this country. They function in the province of Quebec, and are certified for that purpose.
I think it is time that the federal Minister of Labour and his department began to check to find out exactly what is taking place in that province. The time has long since passed in Canada or elsewhere on the north American continent when a company may deny elementary rights granted by law for the protection of workers who wish to organize and can legitimately do so under the law. In my opinion this action places the provincial police of the province of Quebec in the category of hired thugs. It is time we got rid of that kind of thing and brought home to Mr. Duplessis the fact that he is living in Canada and not in some totalitarian country where he can kick people around the way he is doing now.
I should like to say a few words on the question of union security, because it is one of the main issues in the Johns-Manville strike.
This union was certified as the legitimate bargaining agency, but when the strike began the provincial government, through their provincial labour board, immediately cancelled the certification of the union. When they did so, it meant that according to the laws of Quebec they are not the legitimate bargaining agency, and are denied the right, even under the laws of that province, to seek redress of their grievances. On the question of union security I am not going to express my own opinion. I am going to read an article on union security by Andre Laurendeau in Le Devoir of March 8, 1949. The reason I want to put this article on the record is that it is written by someone living in that community. It represents the viewpoint of a Frenchman in Quebec who is progressive. He writes this article on union security in the light of the

Strike of Asbestos Miners strike that is taking place there at the present time. The union is not asking for anything that has not been granted to practically every other union in Canada, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia. It is asking for the Rand formula, and there is nothing unreasonable about that, because it has been adopted in Ontario. A Conservative government is in power there, and they do not go too far in these matters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: You can say that again.

maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
I want to quote from the newspaper article of March 8 of this year, to which I have referred:
Experience proves that without special clauses for union security it is impossible for groups of workers to live in order and security. It is necessary therefore to find ways which will assure the permanency of the union. There are many kinds of them, from union preference and maintenance of membership to the closed shop.
The first reaction of management is to say: But what! I am no longer master of my own enterprise. Then some employers have found that even the closed shop can bring advantages to them, when they treat with a union of good faith; it assures them in effect the stability of labour, gives a sense of responsibility to the union, and suppresses that anarchic condition where a labour organization believes it is forced to resort to demagoguery and agitation to justify its existence and assure its permanence. Are these clauses legitimate? The commission states categorically: "These clauses are all morally legitimate in themselves ..."
It is clear that we are passing through a social crisis in French Canada. It cannot be regulated by boasting of the quiet of the past, by sabotaging necessary reforms, or by lifting your arms to heaven. We live in a time when nothing is more imprudent than to procrastinate.
The greater part of Europe passed through similar crises long ago. Opportunities often missed and reforms long delayed have become triumphant and disastrous revolutions. The opportunity now presents itself to us. It never has exactly the appearance we would like. Are we going to take refuge behind judicial pretexts and condemn with beautiful serenity people who defend their unions, their health and their life?
It is a good thing that more courageous forces have made themselves heard; a good thing that at this moment a religious commission speaks loud and [DOT]clear; a good thing that the diocesan journal of Bis Excellency the Archbishop of Sherbrooke declared, in comment on the asbestos strike where the certification of the Catholic union has been revoked by the labour relations board;
"As with the disappearance of slavery and serfdom, Catholic workers in their struggle to emerge from the proletariat can expect to meet, from top to bottom of the social scale, incomprehension, opposition, persecution.
"It remains for them to carry off the victory. Truth, justice and right are with them, even if the powerful, the very rich, armed with narrow legal formulas, are against them."
This is the price of social peace.
I do not want to prolong the discussion. I think I have said enough to indicate to the

Minister of Labour that all is not well in the province of Quebec in that particular strike. The province is at least thirty years behind the times in its labour relations. The minister may get up and say that labour relations are the responsibility of the provinces. That is true, but on the other hand there is a motion to go into supply, and we shall be voting money which will affect the whole Dominion of Canada. I feel that it is the responsibility of the minister, in the interests of peace, order and good government, to investigate what has taken place in connection with this dispute, and to use his good offices to settle it in the interests of all concerned.
(Translation):

maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words this afternoon on this matter. However, since my remarks apply especially to Canadians of French origin, I shall speak in French. I deeply regret we have not a French-Canadian C.C.F. member to do so.
I quite understand it was surprising to see that English-speaking Canadians did not attach more importance to the asbestos strike, in view of the incredible tactics resorted to in order to break the strike with the assistance of the Quebec government.
The asbestos industry is important in itself but particularly so because of the fact that the major part of the product is exported. The industry thus helps provide Canada with millions of United States dollars.
The strike affecting 5,000 workers and now seven weeks old does not involve salaries only but also union security and especially such vital matters as the health and security of the workers.
When the strike broke out, Premier Dup-lessis hastened to declare it illegal, while in Quebec the provincial department of labour deprived the Catholic asbestos syndicate of its status as official negotiating agent.
The Hon. Mr. Barrette, minister of labour of the province of Quebec, did not declare himself opposed to that formula. In fact, he repeatedly advised the workers to return to their jobs, insisting that negotiations could not be resumed until workers complied with the law.
The executive of the Confederation of Catholic Workers of Canada have always held that the Johns-Manville Company, which they have always considered especially

as the asbestos cartel, had, in these negotiations, shown an utter lack of good faith, a view which developments since the outbreak of the strike seem to justify.
The asbestos workers have received the support of many groups throughout the province of Quebec. The consensus of opinion is that their strike is just, even if it is not legal, and so those workers have obtained the support not only of their own trade union, the Confederation of Catholic Workers, but also that of two others: the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour. In all labour centres of the province, subscriptions were organized in order to allow those workmen to hold their own and get a square deal. They obtained support not only from union members, but also from the Corporation des Instituteurs of the province of Quebec, as you can see.
The French language newspapers have been fairly sympathetic to their cause. Le Devoir of Montreal took a definite stand in favour of the strikers. Among the clergy itself, many authorities voiced the opinion that the strikers' cause was just and deserved the support of public opinion. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote an article written by Roger Mathieu, in La Presse. Referring to Rev. Camirand, a parish priest, he quotes:
"As a priest it is my duty to preach the practice of all virtues, and I have no right to make an exception in the case of justice. Likewise I consider it my bounden duty not only to forbid my parishioners to act unfairly, but to defend them when they are the victims of unfairness, as in this instance," parish priest Camirand stated to us straightforwardly.
"The Asbestos miners, whom I know well because I am their union chaplain, have been and still are extremely patient and docile. They have not temporarily deprived themselves and their children of their livelihood for the mere pleasure of doing so, but they were forced to take that action by unspeakably provocative tactics. Were I a miner, I would myself be on strike and under the circumstances I would have a perfectly clear conscience. Moreover, although not a miner, I am with them to the very end and they know it," said the priest.

maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
As regards the strikers' behaviour, the parish priest considers it exemplary.
"A few incidents which have been magnified and distorted by interested people, have occurred, but they were only the consequence of exasperating provocations against which the labour leaders and myself cannot, despite our efforts, immunize the strikers," he asserted.
Under the circumstances it is surprising that English-language newspapers have not attached more importance to that conflict
Strike of Asbestos Miners which seriously jeopardizes the interests of workers not only in the province of Quebec but in every other part of this country. It is no less astonishing to note that no voice was raised in the House of Commons to depict the situation and point out the employers' neglect of their workers' welfare, when they feel they have the support of politicians. Mr. Speaker, to understand fully the situation of the asbestos workers, one must know in what frightful conditions, comparable in certain respects to those that obtain in some coal mines, those men have been working for years, when asbestosis and tuberculosis make every year numerous victims among them.
However, Canadian subsidiaries of the American companies which are operating our asbestos industry are doing nothing to remove the causes of so much illness among our workers.
Those companies put profits before workers' health and life, and provincial authorities do not seem anxious to compel those employers to take the elementary safety precautions required for the protection of our workmen. The Workmen's Compensation Act does not provide sufficiently for the very special disease known as asbestosis even though its effects are so nefarious that victims of this dreadful occupational disease end up in dire poverty because they cannot obtain the least compensation from the government.
An investigation on asbestosis was published by Mr. Leduc in Le Devoir. The conclusions of this investigation are quite definite and explicit, but so far no one has referred to them. He proved, by official statistics, that the rate of mortality due to tuberculosis was 60 to 85 per 100,000 while in the aforesaid industries, in the province of Quebec, it would be 300 per 100,000.

I think I should make one or two comments on what has already been said on this subject. Frankly I cannot disagree with any of the basic principles of trade union

I do not need to quote from any document or from any person on the right of a trade union organization to function in this or any other country. I think I have expressed myself in this way before: you might as well try to push back the ocean as try to prevent the legitimate functioning of a trade union because it cannot be done.
We are not all either saints or sinners. When a grave issue such as the one we are discussing at the moment is under consideration, I think a tribute can be paid to both sides-that is, to employers and to good employees. During the war this industry came under my jurisdiction under the War Measures Act. I have some knowledge of the officers of the Catholic syndicate. I have seen that organization grow from what I might say was an infant to a lusty adult. Its officers played a great part during the war in the organizations under my jurisdiction. They were members of the national war labour board and of the wartime labour relations board. At the moment Mr. Gerald Picard, president of the organization, is a member of the Canada labour relations board. They also played their part in other sections of the dominion where their organization flourished.
I think this should be said about labour disputes. You do not get into trouble over the things you have to say; it is the silly things you do not have to say and do say that get you into trouble. If hon. members will forgive a personal reference, I think I have had as much experience as any other man in North America in the adjudication of labour disputes. I know I have been criticized. The portfolio of labour is not one of those in which you can win a popularity contest. No man ever went down in history after being a minister of labour in this country, or in any other one, for that matter. But I believe that, given a measure of good will, much can be done. After all is said and done, it is the simple things that govern the life of a nation or the destiny of a civilization. There is nothing complicated about industrial relations. The yardstick of common sense should be the one employed by all of us. I do not think one gets anywhere by calling a man a communist when one knows he is not a communist. I would rather be governed by the gavel than by the gun. In some of the countries in which our 

communist friends find their spiritual home, it is the gun and not the gavel that governs.
I would rather have an assembly such as this with Mr. Speaker in the chair; I would rather have him say once in a while, "The hon. member is out of order," when the hon. member to whom he refers, knowing he is out of order, insists that he is not. I would rather have trade union organizations in which chairmen or presidents may sit with gavels in their hands and rule over what takes place in those meetings. I have seen-and I am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton South has seen the same thing-the chairman of a meeting with a boilermaker's hammer in his hand.

It may be truthfully said that in the last ten years we have made tremendous strides in the stabilization of conditions in the industrial, commercial and transportation system of this country. I do not think any one person can take all the credit for that. Today, with the exception of the one province which has been mentioned, one which is predominantly agricultural, we have seen the development of departments of labour and conciliation services on a plane which compares favourably with that found anywhere else. I believe I have said on many occasions in the house that I am a great believer in conciliation. So many people seem to want to pass a law to put the other fellow-not themselves-in jail. They think that is the way to settle an industrial dispute. I have never shared that opinion. That is why I can say that I agree with many of the statements made this afternoon by my hon. friends from Cape Breton South, Vancouver East, and Megantic-Frontenac.
When we turn our minds to the subject of partnership in industry we must realize at once that in the last five years we have made tremendous strides in the development of labour-management committees under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Labour. Those committees across Canada run into the hundreds.
Let it be clearly understood that I am taking no sides in the present dispute. There is an old saying: stay in your own back yard.

The Englishman's home is his castle.

speechtext: There is such a thing as justice, though.

maintopic: STRIKE OF ASBESTOS MINERS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Of course there is such a thing as justice. I believe in the rule of law, and without equivocation I can say that this present dispute is completely within the jurisdiction of the provincial government. Let there be no misunderstanding about it. This is not a question of taking sides; it is not a question of saying who is right or who is wrong. We have all expressed our views about the rights of working men and women to organize the unions of their choice. I have been long enough in politics to know that it is far better not to quarrel about the other fellow's jurisdiction.
My department has never refused justice to any organization whether it be one of employers or one of employees. They do not always take our advice, but it is given to them free of charge. They might go to other people to whom they would pay a good deal of money and would not get such good advice.
All I can say is that I do hope this dispute will be settled to the satisfaction of the employees organization, and with due regard to the common sense of the other people concerned. The hon. member who brought this matter to the attention of the house has rendered a service to the people of Canada. We hear it said that eternal vigilance is the price of liberty and freedom, but we have to keep on restating that fact.
Let me repeat that there is no substitute for decency and fair dealing. You can pass all the laws that could be contained under the canopy of heaven, but it will not always get you anywhere. You can pass a law to say that men shall not go on strike; but when you have 20,000 or 30,000 men on the street, what can you do about it? One has to be sensible about these things.
I hope nothing I have said-and I am sure nothing anybody else has said-will impair the possibility of settlement of this dispute, keeping in mind always the fact that it is best to use character as a yardstick, and not the exact legal expressions written into a statute.

Mr. Speaker, there is a grievance in my riding that I should like to air in case I do not get a chance again. This is something in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) will be interested. I refer to the issuance of flying licences to private pilots.
I do not want to take up the time of the house by indicating what the present regulations are, but I am sure hon. members who are familiar with them will agree that a man would have to be a Rhodes scholar to pass examinations. I admit that it is no credit to anyone to be a Rhodes scholar, but that is the kind of qualification required under the new regulations.
These regulations might be necessary as applied to one who was going to fly a jet plane or a bomber for the R.C.A.F., but they are not necessary for a private pilot's licence. We have had many outstanding pilots in Canada. The president of Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited is one of the greatest northern fliers we have ever known in Canada, but I doubt very much if he could pass the examinations at present prescribed. In my

Air Regulations
district we built an airport, by municipal and voluntary effort, without the assistance of any government, and without any subsidy. We have the second largest training school in the province of British Columbia, and there are now some fifteen planes at that airport. But the airport will have to be closed this month unless there are some changes in these regulations, which were prepared by those who have been described by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) as "some of these bureaucrats." I appreciate the fact that many of those who prepared the regulations have flown planes, and some of them gallantly, but that was thirty years ago, and they know nothing about present-day flying.
This is an emergency so far as my riding is concerned. We believe that regulations must be made to see to it that those in charge of planes and entrusted with the lives of others should have every necessary qualification, but we believe also that men who have had thousands of hours of flying time should not be barred simply because they have not had a university education. I am informed by pilots of great experience, of wide knowledge, and with fine records, that these qualifications are not necessary. I think I would be within my rights in reading extracts from the examination that must be passed by one who wants to get a licence as a private pilot, even if he had flown on mercy missions to the Arctic or the Antarctic. Unless I quoted from the examinations themselves I doubt whether any hon. member would believe that such a thing had been set up by bureaucrats who have not been in a plane for the last thirty years. Yet men with records such as these, men with great knowledge of flying, will be required to pass these examinations.
The airport at Chilliwack will have to be closed after $100,000 has been spent. That was our own money; we built the airport without assistance from any government.
Before the last war we fell down badly because we had been too cautious about spending money on national defence. If there is anything that Canada should spend money on, it is the training of fliers. We have young men with ability and initiative not surpassed by those of any other country in the world. That has been demonstrated by the record of the Royal Canadian Air Force. This cadet school in my riding will have to be closed because these examinations require that a man be a former professor of Moscow or somewhere else. Unless action is taken within the next thirty days this important training school will have to go.

Well, evidently the situation was watched more or less closely, among others by Colonel A. L. Barry, who at a meeting of the North Shore Salmon Fishermen's Association on November 13, 1946, said that in spite of restrictions and better protection the salmon fisheries had been on the downgrade for some time, and that there had been a big downgrade since 1936, just at the time Mr. Calderwood said it would be noticed. In view of Mr. Calderwood's report and what has been actually observed, therefore, to say that there is no relation between the lowness of the stocks and the number of fish taken by the drift net fishermen is, I believe, absolute nonsense.
The North Shore Salmon Fishermen's Association of New Brunswick have been calling the attention of the Department of Fisheries to the situation for several years, and asking for action. I propose to read part of a resolution passed on April 27, 1948, and sent to the minister:
Our seashore fishermen, being greatly alarmed at the very rapid decrease in the number of salmon they are catching, believe and allege that this destructive net fishery is causing their greatest loss, and a rapid destruction of the whole salmon fishery, and respectfully urge the honourable minister to order the discontinuance of this destructive drift net fishery at the mouth of the Miramichi river as quickly as possible, as otherwise the members of the association believe that the whole salmon fishery of eastern Canada will be utterly destroyed.
The chairman of the council of the association, Mr. George Gilbert, K.C., of Bathurst, has presented the views of the association to the minister on a number of occasions, but so far as I know no action has been taken. On May 19, 1948, the then Minister of Fisheries wrote a letter to Mr. Gilbert in which he said that the department could not accept the statement of the association that drift net fishing was the cause of the declining run. It will be noted, if that letter from the minister is read, that he does not even admit the drift net fishing is or may be one of the causes of the decline in the run. If drift net fishing is not the cause or one of the causes, I call upon the minister to tell us what is the cause of the decline. Surely he and his advisers should be in a position to tell us, particularly if they say that drift netting is not the cause.
I put these questions to the minister, and I believe I am entitled to an answer: First, what is the cause of the decline in our Atlantic salmon fisheries? Second, why have our Atlantic salmon stocks become so low?
In his study of the salmon fisheries of the gulf of St. Lawrence, to which I have referred, Professor Nobbs evidently agrees with the opinion of the North Shore Salmon
fMr. Hazen.]
Fishermen's Association, for at page 6 of his essay he says:
If your salmon fisheries are to be restored, drift net fishing has to be brought to an end, presumably with appropriate compensation to the owners.
I am not unmindful of the fact that the views of the anglers, the shore fishermen and the drifters are influenced by self-interest. It is only human nature that this should be so. I hold no brief for any of them; I am interested in the conservation and improvement of our salmon fisheries as a national asset. I believe the primary interest of the government in this matter is or should be the maintenance and improvement of the numbers of these fish, which give our fishermen a living and provide the best of food for the public. I believe immediate action is necessary, for the catch is exceeding the present natural increase. As Mr. Calderwood has said, and it cannot be denied, if the catch by nets and anglers exceeds the maximum breeding capacity of the rivers, the utter destruction of the fishery may come with a suddenness that will be tragic.
Matters should not be allowed to drift further. The scientists connected with the department and interested in this matter, it seems to me, are so engrossed in minor details that they have failed to see or appreciate the obvious steps that should be taken to improve conditions. They are like men who cannot see the forest for the trees. There must be some driving force to do what is necessary to improve conditions, and I suggest that the minister should be that force.

The fishermen are becoming very much concerned about it.
During the war, for instance, for twelve months of the year these fish were caught day in and day out, twenty-four hours of the day. These draggers are tearing up the bottom of the ocean around the different islands and destroying the feeding grounds of these herring I mentioned. This is having a very harmful effect upon the fisheries of the bay of Fundy. As I said, I do not intend to hold up these estimates but these matters are very serious to the people in that section of the country, and I believe the Department of Fisheries should give them very serious consideration.

I quite agree with all the members who have spoken about this matter, and some work has been done in connection with it. We have two boats busy exploring the herring situation and we believe we know pretty well what has happened to them. I think we can give a good report.

Supply-Fisheries
Representations have been made, then?

Representations have been made and the work of studying the problem is continuing. An outline of that could quite easily be given on item 586.
The second item, item 585, $50,000, is for work on the Nanaimo research station. The work progressed more rapidly than was estimated and this item is to take care of that increase. It will also mean a decrease in the estimates for 1949-50. Have these items carried, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall item 584 carry?

No. I should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries to make a statement about the situation with regard to the marketing of canned salmon from the Pacific coast. As he knows, that is the main fisheries product of the west coast. To illustrate that point I produce a half-page advertisement under the signature of the minister which appeared in one of the Vancouver newspapers last Tuesday. It contains a large drawing of a salmon and reads:
In honour of a fish that helped build a prosperous province!
Probably no statue will ever be erected to honour the B.C. salmon.
Yet monuments in bronze and marble have been raised in tribute to generals, statesmen, industrialists and others whose contributions to public welfare and progress were no greater than the achievements of the humble salmon.
Generals win wars? The salmon served with distinction on all fighting fronts through two great wars, as a nourishing, easily transported food.
Statesmen build nations? The salmon serves Canada in two ways: As a dependable domestic source of tasty, economical meals . . . and as a major export bringing in valuable foreign exchange.
It would appear that the humble salmon has become a casualty in recent months, so far as the west coast variety is concerned. This question is of very great importance to the whole economy of British Columbia. Our main market for canned salmon has been the United Kingdom. Other very important markets were Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. I have here a copy of a speech made by Mr. J. M. Buchanan who until recently was, I believe, the president of the Fisheries Council of Canada. Speaking last summer he gave the figures for the pre-war distribution of the British Columbia pack as approximately: Canada, 35 per cent; the United Kingdom, 23 per cent; Australia and New Zealand, 20 per cent; Africa, 3 per cent; other British empire countries, 3 per cent; other export markets, 16 per cent. Those were the pre-war figures, and the minister can correct me if Mr. Buchanan's figures are out of line. The fact is that the British market has

been our main export market for canned salmon. It is notable that during the war canned salmon could not be obtained at all by civilians in Canada.
It was all requisitioned and shipped to England.

The whole pack was either shipped to England or supplied to the Canadian forces. Mr. Buchanan gives those figures too. He says:
Of the 1941 to 1946 packs, 7,600,000 cases (or 80 per cent) were used for the forces or shipped to the order of Great Britain for overseas needs.
Then he goes on to say:
Probably no other similar food industry made the same sacrifice in its domestic market.
A year or so ago it became obvious that the overseas market for canned salmon was falling off. We on the coast hoped that the Marshall plan would enable European countries to buy our canned salmon. I have here a dispatch of April 8, 1948. The heading is "Marshall Plan may aid Province's Industries". With regard to salmon its says:
Canned salmon, one of the province's big natural crops, was being faced with declining dollar holdings in the United Kingdom and other markets, and looked as if it might become a surplus at home.
Both the salmon and the herring catches, which are much more than can be used in Canada, will probably be needed to supply foodstuffs to Europe.
The belief was that the Marshall plan would mean that our market in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe would be continued. But the situation became steadily worse, and I find here a clipping of January 21, 1949, again in the Vancouver press. The heading is "Salmon Gets Last Chance" and the first paragraph reads as follows:
Fisheries Minister R. W. Mayhew has begun last-chance negotiations toward agreement for sale of British Columbia canned salmon to the United Kingdom, and upon his success or failure will depend to great extent the prosperity of this province's fishermen in 1949.
The next day we had a press dispatch to the effect that Ottawa might agree to accept sterling currency for British Columbia salmon. But on January 27 a further dispatch appeared reporting an interview with William F. Bull, who apparently is director under the Export and Import Permits Act. Mr. Bull said in Vancouver that one of his headaches was what to do about a market for British Columbia's tinned salmon. The dispatch reads in part as follows:
"Talks are now under way in London, but we don't know the answer," he told members of the shipping and foreign trade bureaux of the Board of Trade Wednesday. British commonwealth countries took from 50 to 60 per cent of British Columbia's tinned salmon prior to the war. But this year it was feared they might take none.
Then the next development was a statement by Sir Stafford Cripps reported in the

Canadian press of February 22 of this year. He had this to say with regard to canned salmon being purchased from Canada by Great Britain:
"Normally we buy canned salmon from Russia or timber from Scandinavia or bacon from Poland because we can pay for it in sterling, whereas similar Canadian supplies would cost us dollars."
The canned salmon market has now been cut off completely. I have here a further dispatch of March 23, just ten days ago, which again appeared in the British Columbia press, and which reads in part as follows:
Fishing, among B.C.'s top four industries, faces a threat of disaster this year due to failure of last-minute negotiations for sale of canned salmon to the United Kingdom.
A surplus of 250,000 cases is now backed up in warehouses and a pack of 1,500,000 cases was expected this year. This may be sharply cut by lack of markets.
B.C. Packers'-
That is the largest fish company in British Columbia.
-vice-president R. E. Walker says "if we don't get rid of present stocks, fish prices will drop this season -enough to put many small fishermen out of business."
I am afraid that is an accurate description of the situation. We have this difficulty with regard to selling the salmon in the United States: there is a tariff of 25 per cent against our canned salmon. It is so high that I believe it is practically impossible to get the canned salmon into that market. So unless the Minister of Fisheries has some hopeful news for us today, it looks as though the fishing industry in British Columbia will be hard hit during the present year. You will have noted, Mr. Chairman, that there is quite a large carryover from last year and a large pack is expected again this year!
I have no doubt that the minister has given deep consideration to the problem. Different solutions have been suggested. One is that Canada accept payment in sterling. Another is that some arrangement be made for exchanging our goods for goods produced by Great Britain; for example, exchanging canned salmon for steel produced in the old country. The suggestion has also been made that the government should take steps to underwrite the 1949 pack. Those are various remedies that have appeared in the press from time to time. I am not at the moment advocating any one of them, but I suggest to the minister and to the committee that it is absolutely imperative that a market be found for this canned salmon. It looks as though the situation may be disastrous; I hope it will not be. I am afraid, however, that the situation is bad. Certainly there is a serious problem to be met in this particular industry.
Supply-Fisheries

The situation with regard to canned salmon, Mr. Chairman, is not as hopeless as the hon. member for Vancouver South would indicate in his remarks. About 200,000 cases of chum salmon are left with the industry. What they are concerned about now is the 1949 pack. Negotiations have been going on with the British ever since last fall. Two delegations have been over there to see what could be done. Up to the present time the British have pretty well refused to buy the salmon because they want other goods in preference to the salmon, on the same basis as they do their apples. But I have every reason to hope that something will be done that will enable the British Columbia people to sell a good portion of their salmon in England for this next year.
I do not wish to say anything more about it than that at the present time. We know the situation and we are keeping closely in touch with it; when I say "we", I mean this department, the Department of Trade and Commerce, and also my friends in the Department of Finance. This part of the industry will not be overlooked, and the fishermen are not going to be ruined at all.
Has any consideration been given to taking sterling for the 1949 pack?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I could answer that. As I said before in the house, taking sterling for part of the 1949 pack is nothing more or less than extending further credit to the United Kingdom.
Plus saving our industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Plus taking an exchange risk. If we extend further credit I can see no purpose in extending credit in sterling, which involves not only lending money but taking an exchange risk as well. It may be that salmon could be sold on credit; that is a matter of policy. But there is nothing to be gained by taking sterling. If individual packers are prepared to sell their salmon, take sterling for it and hold the sterling, they would be permitted to do so. But I do not believe they would want to do that.
The reason would be that the individual packers do not consider sterling is worth $4.03; is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is for the individual
packer to answer, not for me.

I have become interested in this discussion, although I live in the interior of Canada. Would the minister tell us what measures he has adopted to arrest the deterioration of the salmon situation of the Atlantic, which was discussed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert.

Supply-Fisheries
If we are going to get into a full-dress debate on the administration of fisheries, then we will certainly not get through these few estimates this year-or today, I should say.
Right the first time.

I suggest that they be referred to at the proper time, upon which occasion all answers can be given. The problem in the east is entirely different from that in the west. In the east it is a lack of salmon, and in the west it is too much salmon. We cannot resolve all those points here.

Mr. Chairman, the confusion in which I find myself is not entirely due to certain hospitality extended to us last week. I find that these are called the further supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1949. Perhaps the Minister of Finance would enlighten me on a point which is causing me some concern. While I speak only from memory, I think this is an unusual procedure. Here in this fiscal year 1949-1950 we find ourselves asked to pass estimates for the preceding year. I know this matter was discussed on another item called a few days ago.
May we not assume that these moneys as set out in this little booklet-and I notice it runs into substantial figures; one item alone accounts for many millions of dollars-have been spent; or have the commitments been made in these amounts? Then, if that is so- and it must be; there cannot be any other answer for it-does it not sound sort of foolish that this committee of the whole of the House of Commons, after the ending of the financial year, should be passing estimates for the year which died only a few days ago. Am I correct in my assumption that that is exactly what we are doing at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I am sure the hon. member knows, the answer is that for many years, perhaps since confederation, so far as the payment of accounts is concerned we have operated on a thirteen-month basis. Throughout the month of April payments are made for accounts relating to the preceding fiscal year. Government books are kept open, and have always been kept open until the end of April, and payments made in April are made with respect to obligations incurred in the preceding year.
I am told that this procedure is not unusual. The final supplementary estimates for the year are brought down almost invariably before the end of the fiscal year, and would not be passed until the early part of the following fiscal year. In the case of these estimates, it is clear that with the month of April being the month in which

payment is to be made, they would have to be passed before the end of April. In the present instance it is hoped they will be passed this week, before parliament adjourns for the Easter recess. That is in conformity with the usual procedure.
Turning to the second question, it is true that a large part of these estimates relates to what might be described as commitments which have been made. The first of the large items is that of the Canadian National Railways. This item is invariably voted in the final supplementary estimates-if there is a deficit.
The other major item is that concerning the wheat board. It represents the cost of a subsidy on feed which went into domestic use. In order to enable the wheat board to pay the farmers for whom it has acted as agent the full price of $2 a bushel, or whatever the amount may be, this vote is offered. Those are the two major items.
None of these payments has been made, unless items are being specifically voted to reimburse payments made out of contingency votes, or votes for unforeseen expenditures. Very frequently we will make urgent payments out of one or other of the votes set up for unforeseen contingencies. Then, as a matter of correct procedure, we bring in a specific item in the final supplementary estimates, and obtain a specific vote from parliament to cover those items.
With those reservations, these supplementary estimates represent the final toting up at the end of the year of what is needed to cover the services of the government during that year; and I am informed it is quite usual that the formal vote should be put through in the early days of the new fiscal year.

Do I understand there is no commercial fishing in the Hudson bay area? I ask that question, because I notice in the press that a commercial organization is going to that section to kill white whales for their oil. I suppose this product would be used in the manufacture of margarine. When I visited that section last the white whales were an attraction for tourists. I understand this commercial organization goes out in canoes with Indian guides or Eskimos to shoot and harpoon the whales. I wonder if we are paying out money to attract tourists, and then throwing away one of our attractions. My understanding is that these whales are first shot and then harpooned. I wonder if the minister would answer that question?

There are no commercial fishermen going to Hudson bay, so far as I know. Last year we did send up a boat to

do some fishing so that the Eskimos in there might have food. However, there is no commercial fishing.
Then, has the minister's department issued a permit for commercial fishing up there, or does it have to issue a permit?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to address the Chair when he speaks.
I did at first.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It is difficult to give each member an opportunity to speak if hon. members, upon rising, do not address the Chair.
I apologize; but I should like to follow up my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Skeena.

I have sat back listening, and had accepted the minister's explanation that actually this is not the time for a general discussion. However, there seems to be a general nervousness in the air that we might not have an opportunity for this discussion at a later date.
No, no.

Events might develop as a result of which discussions of a more vital nature would ensue. I believe the Department of Fisheries should have played a stronger hand in connection with what might be called the decentralization of the halibut fishing season on the Pacific coast, or breaking it down to cover a greater portion of the year. At the present time the process of going halibut fishing is like taking part in a stampede or a gold rush. The season extends for only thirty days. Men have to work all hours, and any breakdown of equipment is vital, so far as making the season pay is concerned. I realize there are certain international features in connection with this matter, but I believe the department should give more consideration to the halibut fishermen on the coast than they have in the past. In the main the present situation is due to the difficulties in marketing, but I shall not go into that any further.
One of these days we will have a marketing crisis in connection with our fish generally and things may reach the point where the prices support board will have to take on the task of the handling and marketing of fish just as the wheat board does with wheat. If there is another glut in this industry, such as was caused last year when there was a washout on the main lines of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, a serious situation will arise.
Supply-Fisheries
If the government is interested in staving off a general crisis in the halibut fishing industry it should step into the picture now. I realize that the government is opposed to the principle of the state-handling of products, but if this crisis develops any further that is the position they will be driven into.

The halibut on the west coast is handled by the international halibut commission and we have not a great deal to say about it. I find that many of the functions of this department have been transferred to boards and commissions and many times we get blamed for things that we have very little to do with. There is nothing that I can say at the present time about halibut except that negotiations are going on and recommendations will be made in due course. Unless we make a sudden call on the country there will be further opportunities before this house to discuss this matter. I hope that the house will take a greater interest in fishing this year because that lack of interest in the past has made it difficult to get things really going. If hon. members on all sides of the house and people throughout the country generally would take an interest in fishing, if they would realize that this industry brings in $200 million a year, much more could be done.
A short time ago the Fisheries Prices Support Act was used to purchase fish in Manitoba and I should like to know if a loss has been suffered in that connection and, if so, how much7

April 9 is the last day on which we take delivery and up to Saturday morning no fish had been delivered. Any fish that come in will have to come in this week and until after the ninth of this month I could not give a satisfactory answer as to what volume will be handled.

I should like to assist the minister not only by taking an interest in his department but in many other ways. The question I should like to ask now is closely related to the one asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South. In view of the situation with regard to canned salmon there is much uncertainty among fishermen on the Pacific coast as to the policy of the government with regard to the export of fresh and frozen salmon. I am sure that if the minister could indicate what the policy will be this year and whether there will be any changes from last year, he will help to stimulate interest in his department.

Last year there was an embargo on certain species of fish caught on the Pacific coast. The matter has not yet been submitted to my colleagues and when

Supply-Fisheries
the time comes to make a decision it will be made known.

The Eskimos and Indians in the Hudson bay district live on white whales-it is one of their main sources of food-while the blubber is used to feed their huskies. I think the minister should check to see that these whales are not cleaned out altogether by commercial fishermen.

Item agreed to.
Special-
586. To provide for assistance in meeting transportation costs of frozen herring that may be purchased in British Columbia by persons, associations or companies for bait in the 1948-49 winter fishery off Nova Scotia, $66,000.

I wanted to say a few words on 585, but perhaps I can work them in under this item. In connection with these supplementary estimates the department seems to be imitating the lobster. As most hon. members know, the lobster always moves backwards, and the department seems to be moving backward in connection with these estimates. We have not yet had the main estimates and here we are dealing with supplementary estimates. We are told that they are last year's estimates, but there is $100 million to be voted. I suppose $100 million is nothing when there is a surplus of $500 million or $600 million.
It is a good thing they mention winter fishery off Nova Scotia in the details of this item. I was wondering what kind of bait this was, whether it was election bait or fishing bait. We will require considerable information on this item. Where was this bought? What fishing associations demanded the purchase of frozen herring in British Columbia to be shipped to the east? Was the herring paid for out of this $66,000, or is this amount just for the freight? How many carloads were shipped and to whom were they consigned? How much freight was paid on a minimum car of 30,000 pounds? If we knew that we would know how many cars had been shipped. To whom was this fish shipped and how was it distributed? Was it shipped to Halifax or to other ports? I may have some further questions to ask, but I should like to have these answered now.

This item is to cover freight on frozen herring from the Pacific to the Atlantic coast. When I visited the eastern coast last fall, and Prince Edward Island, there were a number of people making complaints about the shortage of bait. They claimed that they were about two million pounds short at least, and that unless the catch of herring was pretty substantial in the fall they would be entirely without bait.

When I left the maritime provinces I went to British Columbia and inquired of the fishermen there at what price they could land frozen herring if it became necessary to send it to the east. In Prince Edward Island they told me they were paying as high as 11 cents a pound for herring. In Nova Scotia they were paying between six and seven cents, and in some cases as high as nine cents a pound. The packers on the west coast said that they would be able to load on cars frozen herring of the quality desired by the fishing industry on the east coast for $60 a ton. That is as far as I went with them. We advised the trade that if, through their own trade channels, they placed orders in British Columbia for the fish it could be procured at the price of $60 a ton. The fishermen of the east coast then said to the department that $60 a ton plus 3J cents a pound for freight would still make the cost of the bait too high for commercial fishermen, and they asked the government to pay a subsidy for the freight. The government saw fit to agree to that, and paid the subsidy that is set out here.
The amount of fish that went forward from the Pacific coast to the Atlantic coast was approximately 1,800,000 pounds. The item here is for the freight only. The method of distribution was that we simply advised those wanting these fish that they could place their orders with certain companies in British Columbia. They looked after their own buying and their own distribution just as they would if the fish had been caught in the Atlantic ocean.
Over what period of time have these deliveries been made? Can the minister tell us when the deliveries started, and whether they are completed now?

The deliveries are concluded. They started fishing on the 4th of January, and they fished until they had caught the two million pounds originally provided for. The area in which these fish were caught was on the east side of Vancouver island. If they had tried to fish on the west side the herring would have cost about $10 a ton more. Deliveries were completed some time ago.
Have all deliveries been made where contracts were arranged for this year?
So far as I know. The government made no contracts. Individuals made their own contracts and made their own purchases. As far as I know all deliveries have been made.

There is one comment I wish to make on this matter. I draw the minister's attention to something which we have already discussed in connection with this situation.

I am sure that no one on this side of the house would think of criticizing the department-and in fact would commend them-for any assistance which has been given, but it is a most serious situation when fishermen on the Atlantic seaboard, with the tremendous development of that industry throughout past years, are now compelled to purchase their bait on the Pacific seaboard and transport it all the way across Canada. Certainly it would suggest that there is something radically wrong with the fishing industry that such a situation should exist. It is not for a layman to suggest what the reasons may be.
I referred earlier to a matter which the member for Royal mentioned this afternoon, the operation of trawlers, which I think is undoubtedly contributing markedly to the difficulties of our fishermen on the Atlantic seaboard. We do not wish to hold up these estimates, but at a later time, when the minister's main estimates are before the house, I will refer to that again.
There is one particular matter to which I wish to draw his attention, a matter to which I have referred in discussions and correspondence with him, and on which I think there is a marked difference of opinion between us. As I said, I am not attempting to hold up these estimates now, but I am suggesting to the minister that, unless some satisfactory arrangement can be made with respect to it, when his main estimates are before the house later on, notwithstanding the fears which someone has suggested, I will have to spend much more time on it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is nothing to fear.

In short, the situation, as far as the inshore fishermen are concerned, is that their bait has disappeared, and it is a strange circumstance. The bait has disappeared apparently at the same time that seiners or trawlers operating from New Brunswick across the bay have been coming into the Annapolis basin and seining up hundreds and thousands of hogsheads of small herring which ultimately are prepared for use as food. I understand from communications I have had from the minister, and undoubtedly he believes this, that his experts have advised him that seining has no effect upon the bait situation. That may be. I quite realize that what may appear reasonable to a layman may not be proven satisfactorily to an expert, but I suggest that it is a strange thing that this has happened.
In December of 1948 and January of 1949 one weir operating in the Annapolis basin caught 400 barrels of bait which was distributed to the fishermen of that district. The seiners appeared from across the bay,
Supply-Fisheries
and immediately the fish disappeared from the weir. I am reliably informed by fishermen, whose names I can give to the minister, that from that time on they have not caught any bait in the weir. Five seiners have been operating in the basin catching these small herring, and three carriers have been transporting them across the bay of Fundy to the canning plant in New Brunswick.
As I said, I am not going to quarrel with the experts, but I suggest to the minister that to the layman there seems to be some cause and effect in this matter. I am not so sure whether the cause and effect may not have some relation to the fact that the man who owns the seiners occupies a position not too many hundred feet away from where we sit at the present time, and is very prominent in the councils of the party opposite. That may not have anything to do with it, but it is a very strange thing that these seiners are permitted to operate when trawlers, as I pointed out before, are forbidden to fish within twelve miles of our coast.
It may be that the fishermen do not know what they are talking about. I can quite believe that they may be honestly mistaken, that there is some scientific explanation, but I suggest to the minister that the easiest way to clean it up is to forbid seiners from operating within the basin. He has the power to do it. The licence can be endorsed as licences are now endorsed to the effect that trawlers are prohibited from fishing within twelve miles of the coast line. Certainly seiners could be prohibited from fishing within a quarter of a mile of a weir operated by inshore fishermen. If that is done for a period of two or three years, and the bait situation remains serious, then the fishermen will have to admit that they are wrong, and they will have to bow to the judgment of the experts. Until that is done they are not going to be satisfied. When you have a situation where the bait has fallen off to less than two per cent of what it was before the seiners arrived, I suggest from a practical standpoint that there is something there which warrants the attention of the minister. I will not take any further time now, but I am telling him seriously that, when this matter is before us again on his other estimates, unless some action is promised probably we shall have to spend much more time on the question than we are taking now.

If you go back through the history of the sardine and herring industry I think you will find that ever since it has been established we have had years when these fish were in very short supply. The past six or eight months has been one of these seasons of scarcity. I know in my

Supply-Fisheries
own county this winter we have been unable to get a supply sufficient to keep the canneries going tor more than one-third of the time. That condition has prevailed on many occasions in years gone by, and I am afraid it will prevail again in future.
I should like to clarify the hon. member's statement in connection with seiners. There are many of these people in my own county. Nine out of ten own their own boats and gear, and you will not find a more rugged bunch of fishermen anywhere in the maritime provinces. If sardines are to be caught at Digby or Grand Manan or anywhere else in the maritime provinces, you will find these boats on the job winter and summer. The hon. gentleman mentioned the sardines taken at Digby. I guarantee that more sardines are taken at Charlottetown in one day than would be caught at Digby in one year; and that happens year after year. I am not saying that purse seining may not be harmful to some extent, in the sardine industry; I am not in a position to argue that point; but this type of fishing has been carried on in my county for about ten years. In 1947 we had one of the biggest years in our history followed by another big year in 1948, but since last December sardines have been very scarce. Just in passing I might say that I remember seeing records which showed that 1890 was a year of great scarcity in the sardine industry on the east coast. At that time there would be no danger of purse seining interfering because then the fish were all caught in sardine weirs.
I wanted to clarify the position of the seiners, most of whom own their own boats and purse seines, and whose equipment is second to none. They are not looking for charity. They are men who are out working winter and summer, doing a very fine job.

I appreciate the fact that the fishermen on the Atlantic coast need bait, and if there is a surplus of herring on the Pacific coast it would be very good practice to send that surplus to the Atlantic. We want to be quite certain, however, that in so doing we are not depriving industries on the Pacific coast, and that we are getting a fair price for the herring shipped to Nova Scotia for use as bait. The price mentioned by the minister of $60 a ton is only about half the normal price paid on the Pacific coast for frozen herring, since 5 cents a pound is regarded as about normal.
The sale of herring for use as bait is by no means the only use made of that catch. After receiving various letters from feed merchants on Vancouver island, both in my own constituency and the constituency repre-

sented by the minister, in regard to the difficulty of getting fish meal, a few days ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question about the supplies of that commodity. On March 31, after having consulted the officials of his department, he stated that in comparison with the last two or three seasons, comparatively few herring had been canned, the catch being used mainly for oil and meal. He said almost 31,000 tons of fish meal were produced, the highest on record, and that supplies for the market served by the Pacific coast fisheries were good. Prices remained firm, indicating that the demand is also good.
I would like to call attention to the fact that only small quantities have been canned, and that comparatively few herring have been used for the production of fish meal. I said I had received letters from feed merchants on the Pacific coast pointing out that they were short of fish meal for use in poultry laying mash. In a letter I received only a few days ago I am told that they now have to pay $200 a ton for fish meal, which is about twice what had to be paid for this product only a couple of years ago. I have another letter telling me of the prices now asked for laying mash of which fish meal is an essential ingredient. In 1947 such mash was sold at the feed stores for $49 a ton. This year it is $85 a ton; in other words it has almost doubled in price in two years. I know there are many reasons for this, and certainly one of those reasons is the shortage of fish meal and the increase in price. That results from the fact that only a small share of the herring caught on the Pacific coast is being used to produce a commodity which is urgently needed in that area.
Then again, the fish salteries on the gulf islands in my constituency, where herring were dried, salted, cured and shipped to China, are all idle. They have been closed for many years. Inquiries were made as to whether or not it would be possible to revive that industry, which might open up a better market for the fishermen than having the herring shipped to the Atlantic coast for use as bait, which would also entail the payment of transportation charges by the government. That might be well worth investigating. Then I feel that we must take very seriously the warning given by the previous speaker with respect to the use of various types of trawlers in the waters around Vancouver island. I know the officials of the minister's department have been con-. sidering for a number of years whether or not limitations should be placed on the auto trawlers and beam trawlers which operate between Vancouver island and the mainland. Not only the fishermen but also many scientists claim that these trawlers are doing con-

siderable damage to young herring spawn in these waters. Certain prohibitions have been imposed upon the use of the auto trawler in these particular waters off the east coast of Vancouver island, from which these herring are shipped. I do think we should take very seriously the warning which has been given from the Atlantic coast where, owing to the use of certain types of fishing equipment, they have lost their catch of bait. We have to take what must be considered an uneconomical step by shipping bait from the Pacific to the Atlantic coast. If we are not careful we shall find we are in exactly the same position on the Pacific coast. If steps are not taken to conserve the catch of herring and prevent that type of fish from being destroyed when they are immature, that is what will happen.
I would therefore ask the minister to give very careful consideration to the various points I have raised, namely, that this is not the most economical or the most profitable means of handling our herring on the Pacific coast; secondly, that the fact that we are exporting such great quantities of herring from the Pacific coast has created a shortage of poultry food which is urgently needed by the poultry producers on the Pacific coast; thirdly, the question of conserving our herring by prohibiting the use of destructive equipment in those waters in which the herring remain.

I think I should answer the hon. member's question, although I do not want to delay my own estimates. He is quite wrong in most of what he has had to say, but probably that is due to Easter coming or lent being over. The fishermen did not catch less fish because of these 1,800,000 pounds of herring that went to the east coast. They had their full quota. Our boats explored the situation on both the east and the west coasts and it was our belief that we could reasonably let this quantity of herring go to the Atlantic coast for bait. In addition to that, the season was lengthened and some 40,000 tons extra were caught on the west coast, so that they got more than their ordinary quota. Most of that went into bait and into cans. I was not aware that any of it went into oil cans. They had a carryover from last year and that is the reason there was none put up this year.
I believe this was a proper act. When there was a shortage of bait on the Atlantic coast it was proper for us to ship this bait to them at the prices that were obtained and I would be very glad to do it again. I only hope that the time never arrives when we shall have to request something from the Atlantic coast. I remember quite well that there were years when the herring on the
Supply-Fisheries
Pacific coast were in short supply. This year there was a phenomenal run of herring on the Pacific coast but there were few on the Atlantic coast.

Perhaps the minister would inform the committee whether any arrangements are being made for the repayment of this vote. Is this money being made available to the fishermen of Nova Scotia to go fishing with British Columbia bait or is it an outright gift? Is the government now supplying bait so that fishermen can go fishing?

If they have not sufficient bait with which to go fishing, I would be glad to supply it. I would recommend once more that something be done so that the industry on the Atlantic coast could be maintained just the same as the industry on the Pacific coast.
It is public money with which the minister is being so generous. I think he ought to make arrangements to have it returned.
It would be a greater disaster if the people on the Atlantic coast could not fish for want of bait.

It is my understanding that, unfortunately, the maritimers did not have the necessary bait. I can quite appreciate the fact that these fishermen would not have as good a catch with maritime bait as they would have with bait from British Columbia. I want to point out that my understanding of this is that through some misunderstanding or some mistake, not on the part of the government or of the federal department of fisheries, these fishermen did not have bait reserved. Of course we appreciate, Mr. Chairman, that with British Columbia bait you could catch more fish than you could with bait from any other place in the world. I believe the government of Canada paid a subsidy of so much a pound to provide the necessary bait so that the maritime fishermen would be able to carry on and support their families for the rest of the year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
May I just say a few words on this question. The circumstances this year were unusual and there was a great shortage of bait. Next year there might be an overage. The minister certainly did the right thing in rendering this assistance, just as the dominion government rendered assistance at the time of the disastrous floods in the Fraser valley or for prairie farm rehabilitation or anything else that might be needed from time to time to provide assistance which cannot be provided by the individual.
I might also say that 1,800,000 pounds of herring is not a tremendous quantity. The

Supply-Labour
supplies on the west coast have not been materially decreased. I congratulate the minister on the forethought he has shown, which has enabled our fishermen to continue their work until such time as they too have large quantities of herring. Perhaps some day the maritimes will be able to supply the west coast with herring. I can tell you we will be very glad to sell them to you if we have any.

Is this subsidy going to be continued? I just answered a telephone call a few moments ago from the fishermen's union and they desired to know whether they could still take advantage of this and continue to get bait for the next month?
I understand there is plenty of bait in Newfoundland. No herring are running on the west coast now and what herring we have would not be suitable for bait. It will therefore have to be discontinued.
