That applause is most expressive evidence of the reason why this committee should get some information about what it is discussing. The Minister of National Defence has not attempted to deal with this subject. All he has done is simply to say that these answers cannot be given. This committee is being asked to deal with a subject as important as this with nothing but vague and utterly meaningless assurances by the Minister of National Defence. When this matter comes up again I am certainly going to ask for a standing vote as an expression of support or otherwise for the demand that a standing committee be set up to discuss our defence preparations.

There is one fact which stands out quite clearly as a result of this discussion, that there is a real point to be considered in whether or not there should be set up a committee on national defence matters. The Minister of National Defence has intimated that such a committee could not be set up under our present methods of procedure.
I would point out to him that just two or three years ago we set up a committee on external affairs, a new committee since the war. I do not think anyone will question the assertion [DOT] that that committee has been most successful. Leading civil servants have appeared before it, such as General McNaugh-ton, who was before the committee about two years ago. The under secretary of state for external affairs has appeared there at different times, and the results have been very beneficial. We ask for a committee of the same type on matters of national defence. I am sure that the Minister of Finance will remember that, when he was Minister of National Defence, the same proposal was made to him. At that time he intimated that he could see no objection to the setting up of a standing committee, and I think perhaps if he had continued as Minister of National Defence we would have had one. Further, the former Prime Minister, the present member for Glengarry, made the same statement to the effect that he thought it might be a very good idea to have a committee of this house to deal with matters of national defence.
In this present year of 1949 defence questions are of steadily increasing importance. I know that the Minister of National Defence wants to maintain the interest, not only of members of the house but of the public, in the armed forces. Yet under the present method of dealing with defence estimates we can only have a very hit-or-miss discussion across the floor of the house. It cannot be carried on in an effective, businesslike way. The result is that few members pay much attention to the question. Very few members

Supply-National Defence study the problems of defence and the best way of strengthening our defence forces. I suggest to the minister that, in the interests of his own fighting forces, it would be all to the good to have a committee of this house before whom the chiefs of staff, or other leading officers, could appear. Members of the different parties serving on that committee would become greatly interested in defence matters. The result would be an increase right across the country in the support for our defence forces.
I make these suggestions in the utmost sincerity, and in the belief that the result would be a strengthening of our forces. I think another result would be to make the minister's work a great deal easier. In the few minutes that this discussion has been going on, I have not been able to find the discussions of other years. I do not believe, however, that there is very much opposition in the house to the setting up of a committee. Members must be at least half convinced that it would be a good thing to have a committee of the house on defence matters. I hope that the minister will not take an adamant stand this evening, and decline to give the proposal any further consideration. I am quite sure that it would be a great help to the whole country.

In answering the leader of the opposition the minister suggested that the charge that our defence forces are inadequate, and that proper disclosure has not been made, is a vague one. The minister also suggested that to give this information would be to aid the enemy and not to aid ourselves. When it is charged that the minister and the government are cloaking behind the suggestion of military security or secrecy their failure to provide Canada with even a minimum of the standing forces needed to beat back the minister's own idea of a diversionary attack, what is vague about that charge? I think when such a charge is made it is most necessary that the minister disclose this information to parliament and to the Canadian people. When we are dealing in figures that are below minimums it is much more important that the people of Canada should be informed than that we should consider what kind of aid we may be giving to a possible enemy. A possible enemy will not get any information of any value from the fact that the government has fallen so far behind a target which is inadequate in any event.
The minister suggested that there were no precedents in this parliament for disclosure of this information. Let me give him a few very specific precedents. He claimed that the answer to the question referring to the number of parachutists in the P.P.C.L.I. would, if it were given, eventually disclose the entire 
battle order and fighting strength of the Canadian forces. On page 1713 of Hansard of the second session of 1945 the then Minister of National Defence disclosed in detail the battle order of this brigade group. He gave it as headquarters, three infantry battalions, one field regiment, one anti-tank battery, one field company, two armoured regiments, a medium battery and an anti-aircraft battery. I do not think there could be much more complete disclosure of the order of battle.
In 1947 at page 5327 of Hansard for that year the present Minister of National Defence gave for that time exactly the information asked for by the hon. member for Calgary East in his second question. The second question is, what is the strength of the active force, Canadian army brigade group, as of February 15, 1949, or the nearest date to that for which returns have been made? In 1947 the Minister of National Defence said that it then consisted of 192 officers and 1,952 other ranks, that he had set a quota on it of 3,541 officers and men, and that its full strength would be approximately 5,000 officers and men. There is a precedent in the Canadian parliament from the mouth of the present Minister of National Defence, who in 1947 answered this very question.
The Minister of National Defence said that if an enemy was contemplating a diversionary raid on this country, that enemy would like to know nothing better than the strength which was available to oppose him. I do not think that any aggressor, and particularly an aggressor that has as large an armed force as this one, and is as far away as it is, will ever figure as closely as the answer to the question asked. I should think that the information contained in a Canadian press dispatch of January 4, 1949, which presumably emanated from the minister's office, or from the public relations branch of the armed services, would be quite adequate for the purposes of any would-be aggressor. Dealing with the brigade group there is this paragraph:
The last of the new pieces of equipment to come into the limelight is the American Fairchild Packet transport plane that will be used by the airborne brigade, which the government has said will be a standing force to meet any diversionary attack on the country. Its eventual strength has been given as 7,000 men, including three battalions of infantry.
Defence Minister Claxton said recently it should begin training as a formation some time this year but that may be a bit optimistic if the entire formation is included.
I wonder what more an aggressor would need than the mere perusal of press reports which have come out of the minister's office with regard to this brigade group. Then as to the number of people trained as parachutists, I have not seen a statement by the minister giving any figures, but in a report

appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of December 28, 1948, I have a statement by the minister to this effect:
In the training of the army's out-size airborne brigade, extra attention would be paid to airborne and Arctic fighting. For the first time, Canadian infantrymen would study fighting under Arctic conditions at the Churchill, Manitoba, experimental base this winter.
That very statement suggests, of course, that up to this time Canadian infantrymen have not engaged in the study of fighting under Arctic conditions, which I should think might be a very important bit of information given by the minister to this would-be aggressor. Then the statement goes on:
There also would be an enlargement of the size of classes taking paratroop training at Rivers, Manitoba.
There you have the name of the base for parachute training, and the suggestion that this year there is going to be an enlargement of the intake for that training. I suggest to the minister that to say the information requested in this question should not be given, when he has volunteered other information about future intentions probably much more important than the actual strength of our forces as of today, is quite ridiculous. I think the precedents I have brought before the committee tonight show clearly that the reason the government does not want to give this information is that it is ashamed of the progress it has made in the recruitment of this brigade group and our regular air force.
I do not want to suggest for a moment that this is any fault of the defence forces themselves; in fact I am perfectly certain it is not. After all, the three defence forces must work under the direction of the minister and the government. If the minister provides them with target strengths adequate for expansion, then they can be expected to provide the training and recruitment facilities to reach those target strengths. If on the other hand the minister cuts down the target strength so they cannot recruit up to the numbers they would like to have, then quite obviously they will provide training establishments and equipment upon the scale permitted to them by the minister. The house knows that in 1947 the minister imposed a limitation upon the size of our armed forces; that is, seventy-five per cent of authorized strength. The result of that limitation certainly must have been that the defence forces cut back their provision for training facilities. Obviously it would be foolish to plan on training a very large number of men if the government was not going to permit the forces to recruit beyond a very low limit. Certainly one of the results of that cut-back in 1947 has been that in all three services, from the global
Supply-National Defence figures the minister is always willing to give, recruiting has been very poor, and that their strength is inching upward very slowly month by month.
When I said recruiting has been poor I noticed the minister make a note. I realize that in the last two months, according to an answer he gave the other day, recruiting for the army has stepped up considerably; but in actual fact during the past year there has been an intake of only 3,000 into the active army, only 1,200 into the active navy, and only 2,671 into the active air force. Those figures give members of this house and the people of the country cause for alarm. On the one hand we have statements by the minister and other members of the cabinet about the grave international situation, and on the other hand we see our defence forces progressing so slowly towards strength. According to another press clipping the authorities have stated that it takes twelve to eighteen months to train a force. I should have thought it would take longer than that to train a regular airborne force, but let us take the statement as it stands. If in fact, as I believe, the only active force in the army, the brigade group, is at present under strength, has not done any formation training, has not completed its airborne training and is not provided with transport aircraft to lift it, and if in fact there are not sufficient fighter planes to escort that force should it be required to go anywhere, then I submit that the giving to this house of the accurate information so we can do something about it is much more likely to save the country than aid the enemy.
I could say much more on this question of the strength of our three services, Mr. Chairman, but I rose only to give you and the members of the committee these precedents which the minister said we did not possess.

Before the minister speaks again, there are certain things I believe have not been discussed so far in this debate, and I propose to discuss one of them briefly at this moment. The minister said it had been decided, and I think it is tacitly admitted, that Russia is our only possible potential aggressor, so we have to consider what type of aggression we are likely to meet.
There is a new phrase, a happy little phrase, to which one can give whatever meaning one likes; it is called a "diversionary raid". A diversionary raid may mean anything from an all-out attack to something with which you can cope with forces that are totally inadequate, as most of us believe. There is one weapon which the Russians have spent a great deal of time studying and it is one weapon which we have not got.

Supply-National Defence The minister admitted we have no submarines. It is reported that the minister said if we needed a submarine we could borrow one. I will deal with that statement in a moment, but I should like to say now that since the end of the war Russia has concentrated on two types of weapon: one is the airplane, which has been dealt with by the leader of the opposition, and the other is the submarine.
Today, with the help of German experts the Russians have submarines which are capable of eighteen knots submerged and approximately twenty-eight knots on the surface. This means that corvettes and frigates are completely obsolete. It also means that the fastest liners afloat are no longer safe from submarine attack. With submarines capable of these speeds even liners such as the Queen Elizabeth and the Queen Mary no longer enjoy the immunity they enjoyed during the last war. That is the first thing we must consider, the advantage that speed has given to our potential enemy.
Let us look at the next fact. Modern submarines can stay at sea for weeks and, it is thought, probably months at a time. This enables them to get into position long before any attack is made with the new weapons, which could be an attack either in one place or in a great many places at the same time. The next device with which the modern submarine is equipped, which it did not have during this war is, of course, the schnorkel. Not only does the schnorkel enable the submarine to remain under water for long periods of time but, what was not realized at the time it was invented, it also makes the submerged submarine difficult to detect by the ordinary method of radar from the air. Here you have an under-sea weapon capable of great speed and tremendous destructive power. Ordinary surface vessels are now obsolete. By the use of the schnorkel you have a submarine which it is difficult, if not impossible, to detect from the air.
The only adequate detection of underwater craft at the present time is by means of asdic or what is now called sonar. This is simply-it is, in fact not simple-a method of detecting submarines by an air and echo process. What does this mean? This means that unless a country has submarines to defend itself against the submarines of the enemy, it is more or less defenceless. Really, there is no adequate anti-submarine device. There are listening devices in the harbours, but here again modern technique in the use of submarines has made it extremely easy for submarines to enter harbours, do the damage of which they are capable of doing, and escape.

There is another device with which we are confronted, and that is the long-term mine. Today pressure mines can lie at the bottom of a harbour for periods of up to three months completely undetected until activated. They cannot be dredged nor swept. The only way in which they can be removed is by attacking them under the water. As a matter of fact the only satisfactory method devised has been the use of human divers. This means that, if we have a diversionary attack, mines can be laid in every harbour in the country, mines can be laid in every river in our country, long before any overt act of hostility has taken place. These mines could stay there for periods of months before the diversionary attack took place.
Let us look at the other modern weapons of naval warfare. Those who have seen the results and studied the effect of both the under-water and air atomic bombing at Bikini, both Abel and Baker, realize that the ships sprayed with highly radioactive spray from the water became so hot they were untenable and could not be moved for months -some of them for years. With the use of atomic weapons we are going to find that the surface fleets of the future are extremely vulnerable. Mr. Chairman, unless we have some method of providing for both underwater offence and under-water transportation, we are going to find ourselves in a very serious position.
Recently suggestions have been made for the use of submarines as both cargo and troop carrying vessels. With the modern devices which have been at least hinted, there is no reason to assume that we cannot use submarines for these purposes. At the moment, Mr. Chairman, we have no submarines whatever. The recent manoeuvres in the Atlantic have shown that even some of the smallest submarines of the United States navy were able almost completely to destroy an attacking force. I think only two ships got through. With a weapon such as this, we cannot consider our defences adequate unless we are proficient in its use. Our having no submarines leaves us in the most vulnerable position of any nation. It is true that we could borrow a submarine from the United States; but borrowing a submarine from the United States is like trying to learn to play the piano by borrowing your neighbour's instrument. You do not get very far by that means. The neighbour frequently wants his own piano to play on. Certainly he wants his own submarines if a war is likely or if there is a threat of war.
We said that the building of submarines and the training of submarine crews are com

plicated and expensive matters and that they are a long-term proposition. That is all the more reason why we should have some submarines and should have properly-trained crews. It may surprise this committee to know that in the first great war the first submarines to cross the Atlantic were actually Canadian-built. I think most of them were built at Montreal. They were E-class boats which proved to be efficient, and they stood up extremely well right to the end of that war.
As was shown in the last war, there were in Canada shipyards that had the know-how to build these vessels. I submit that those skills must be restored. Not only must we have the vessels but we must have the crews already trained, because we cannot leave ourselves defenceless against this new type of warfare. We cannot afford to have a defence force without an adequate, well-trained, keen group of submariners. That is the position we find ourselves in today. I realize, Mr. Chairman, that it is an expensive proposition and that it would take time. I realize that the first proto-type submarine we try to build will probably have "bugs" in it and will probably be difficult to perfect. But believe me, Mr. Chairman, it is infinitely better to find out what we don't know when we are still at peace than it is to find out what we don't know when the enemy is at our sea coast.

All hon. members will agree, I believe, that the defence of Canada is an extremely important subject. Personally I regret that it should have come up on this occasion. I think a much better time should have been set aside for the discussion, and that we should have been apprised of that fact beforehand so that we could have come prepared to discuss the subject. We are now discussing only a small item. I notice that the leader of the opposition has argued forcibly that the minister has refused to answer questions. Then the hon. gentleman who supports him and who covered his rear argued and proved by the facts that the minister had answered all the questions. So here we have the situation. I just want to say that, since that has been said-that the minister has refused to answer the questions and that he has answered them all-that squares the whole proposition. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the item before us which provides, [DOT] as I understand it, for the government's contribution to the permanent forces pension fund-
You are wrong.

You have been asleep.
